title: What is the difference between Kafka (distributed log, durable, replay, high throughput, flat topics) vs RabbitMQ (traditional message queue, AMQP, routing keys, exchanges, lower latency per message, no replay) — and when do you use each (Kafka for event streaming/sourcing/big data pipelines; RabbitMQ for task queues/RPC/simple pub-sub with complex routing)?
shortTitle: What is the difference between Kafka and RabbitMQ, and when do you use each?
topicTitle: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS vs Pulsar

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka and RabbitMQ are both messaging systems but with fundamentally different models. Kafka is a distributed, durable, append-only commit log: messages are retained on disk for a configured time and consumers track their own offset, so many consumers can read the same data independently and replay it. RabbitMQ is a traditional message broker implementing the AMQP model: producers publish to exchanges that route messages by binding rules and routing keys into queues, and once a message is consumed and acknowledged it is removed, so there is no replay by default. Kafka favours high throughput and event streaming with flat topics, while RabbitMQ favours flexible routing and low per-message latency for task queues and RPC.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, Kafka is like the bank's permanent transaction ledger: every event is written down in order and kept, and any department can come and read from wherever they left off, even re-read last week's entries. RabbitMQ is like an internal mail sorting room with clever routing rules: a letter is dropped at the sorting desk, the desk decides which pigeonholes it belongs in based on the address labels, and once a clerk picks up their letter and signs for it, it is gone from the pigeonhole. The ledger is about keeping and replaying a stream of events; the mail room is about delivering each task to the right worker and then forgetting it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka is a durable, replayable log for high-throughput event streaming; RabbitMQ is a routing-rich message queue for task delivery with low latency and no replay.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka and RabbitMQ are both messaging systems but with fundamentally different models. Kafka is a distributed, durable, append-only commit log: messages are retained on disk for a configured time and consumers track their own offset, so many consumers can read the same data independently and replay it. RabbitMQ is a traditional message broker implementing the AMQP model: producers publish to exchanges that route messages by binding rules and routing keys into queues, and once a message is consumed and acknowledged it is removed, so there is no replay by default. Kafka favours high throughput and event streaming with flat topics, while RabbitMQ favours flexible routing and low per-message latency for task queues and RPC.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, Kafka is like the bank's permanent transaction ledger: every event is written down in order and kept, and any department can come and read from wherever they left off, even re-read last week's entries. RabbitMQ is like an internal mail sorting room with clever routing rules: a letter is dropped at the sorting desk, the desk decides which pigeonholes it belongs in based on the address labels, and once a clerk picks up their letter and signs for it, it is gone from the pigeonhole. The ledger is about keeping and replaying a stream of events; the mail room is about delivering each task to the right worker and then forgetting it.

**One line to remember:** Kafka is a durable, replayable log for high-throughput event streaming; RabbitMQ is a routing-rich message queue for task delivery with low latency and no replay.

sections.s2_technical:
Kafka's core is an append-only log partitioned across brokers. Producers append records to a topic partition, the records are kept on disk for the retention period regardless of whether anyone has read them, and each consumer group tracks its own offset, which is just a position in the log. This is why Kafka supports replay: a new consumer, or an existing one that resets its offset, can re-read all retained records from the beginning. It is also why Kafka scales to very high throughput, because appending to a log and reading sequentially is extremely efficient, and parallelism comes from partitions. Topics are flat, so fine-grained routing is done consumer-side by filtering or by stream processing, not by the broker.

RabbitMQ's core is the AMQP exchange-and-queue model. A producer publishes to an exchange, not directly to a queue, and the exchange routes the message into one or more queues according to bindings and the message's routing key. A direct exchange matches the routing key exactly, a topic exchange matches wildcard patterns, a fanout exchange broadcasts to all bound queues, and a headers exchange matches on header attributes. Consumers read from queues, and when a consumer acknowledges a message it is removed from the queue. This gives rich, broker-side routing and typically very low per-message latency, but there is no built-in replay, because a consumed and acknowledged message is gone.

The consumption models differ accordingly. In Kafka, consumers pull from the log at their own pace and the data stays, so multiple independent consumer groups each get the full stream, which is ideal for fan-out to many systems and for event sourcing. In RabbitMQ, a message in a queue is typically delivered to one consumer among those competing on that queue, which is the natural task-queue model where you want each job done once by one worker; broadcasting to many consumers requires a fanout exchange binding separate queues. RabbitMQ also has first-class features Kafka does not, like per-message time-to-live, priority queues, and straightforward request-reply RPC with a reply-to queue.

The decision is about the workload. You choose Kafka for event streaming, event sourcing, big-data pipelines, log aggregation, and any case where you need durability, replay, very high throughput, or multiple independent consumers of the same stream. You choose RabbitMQ for task and work queues where each job is processed once, for request-reply RPC, for low-latency delivery of individual messages, and for scenarios needing complex broker-side routing, priorities, or per-message expiry. The senior nuances are that Kafka can emulate a work queue with a consumer group but lacks per-message priority and fine routing, while RabbitMQ can emulate pub-sub with fanout but is not built for long retention or replay or the throughput of a log; that Kafka retains by time or size so replay is bounded by retention; that RabbitMQ streams, a newer feature, add log-like retention but the classic queue model is what distinguishes it; and that many banks run both, Kafka as the event backbone and RabbitMQ for targeted task routing and RPC.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem at National Bank of India is that two different needs were being forced onto one tool, and each needed the strengths of a different system.

Problem 1 — the analytics, fraud, and ledger teams all need to read the complete stream of transaction events independently, and occasionally replay last month's events to rebuild a view. This is exactly Kafka's strength: a durable log where each consumer group reads the full retained stream at its own offset and can replay.

Problem 2 — a loan application must be handed to exactly one back-office worker from a pool to process, and some urgent applications must jump the queue, and a quote request needs an immediate reply. This is exactly RabbitMQ's strength: a work queue delivering each job to one competing consumer, with priority queues for urgent items and request-reply for the quote.

Problem 3 — the two must not interfere, because the streaming backbone should not be burdened with fine-grained routing and the task queue should not try to retain and replay everything.

The code will model a `KafkaLog` with offset-based replayable consumption by multiple groups, and a `RabbitBroker` with an exchange routing by key into queues where a message is consumed once and acknowledged. The demo step is: publish transaction events to the Kafka log and have two independent consumer groups read and then replay them, and publish loan tasks to the RabbitMQ exchange so they route to the right queue, are consumed once by a worker, and disappear after acknowledgement.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql
CREATE TABLE transaction_events (
    offset_no  BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,         -- Kafka-style log position
    txn_id     VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE loan_tasks (
    task_id    VARCHAR(30) PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    priority   VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,        -- RabbitMQ priority queue
    status     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'QUEUED'
);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:                     # durable log: retention + consumer offsets
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    consumer:
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
  rabbitmq:                  # AMQP broker: exchanges + routing keys + queues
    host: localhost
    port: 5672
bank:
  kafka:
    topic: transaction.events
    retention-days: 7
  rabbit:
    exchange: loan.exchange
    routing-urgent: loan.urgent
    routing-normal: loan.normal
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is two transaction events for the Kafka side and two loan tasks for the RabbitMQ side.

Step 1: On the Kafka side, two transaction events are appended to the log at offsets zero and one. They are written to disk and retained, independent of any consumer.

Step 2: The analytics consumer group reads the full stream from offset zero to one. Reading does not remove anything; the records stay on the log.

Step 3: The fraud consumer group reads the same two records independently, from its own offset, getting the complete stream too. This is the multi-consumer strength of a log.

Step 4: The ledger group replays from offset zero, re-reading both records because the data is still on disk, demonstrating replay that a traditional queue cannot do.

Step 5: On the RabbitMQ side, two loan tasks are published to the exchange with routing keys. The exchange routes the urgent task into the urgent queue and the normal task into the normal queue based on the bindings, which is broker-side routing.

Step 6: A worker on each queue consumes exactly one message and acknowledges it, which removes it from the queue. When a worker tries the urgent queue again, it is empty, because the message was consumed once and is gone. The output shows the retained, replayable Kafka log and the routed, consume-once RabbitMQ queues.

```
  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ KAFKA: Log + per-consumer cursor (offset) → replay, fan-out       │
  │ RABBITMQ: Publish-Subscribe via Exchange (router) + Competing     │

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ KafkaLog                 │        │ RabbitBroker              │
  │ - partition: List        │        │ - bindings: Map<key,queue>│
  │ + append                 │        │ - queues: Map<queue,Deque>│
  │ + readAs(group)          │        │ + bind/publish            │
  │ + replayAs(group)        │        │ + worker(queue)           │
  └──────────────────────────┘        └───────────┬──────────────┘
                                                   ▼
                                       ┌──────────────────────────┐
                                       │ QueueWorker               │
                                       │ + consumeOne() → ack/remove│
                                       └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a message ───────────────────────────────────────

  KAFKA record:  [APPENDED] ──read by group A──→ still [RETAINED] ──replay──→ [RETAINED]
                   (removed only when retention expires)
  RABBIT message:[QUEUED] ──deliver──→ [UNACKED] ──ack──→ [REMOVED]
                   (nack/timeout → requeue)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────────

  1. kafka.append x2 → offsets 0,1 (retained)
  2. kafka.readAs(analytics) / readAs(fraud) / replayAs(ledger) → all see full stream
  3. rabbit.publish(loan.urgent / loan.normal) → exchange routes to queues
  4. worker(urgent).consumeOne → ack → removed; retry → empty
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka and RabbitMQ are both messaging systems, but they are built on fundamentally different models, and that drives when I use each. Kafka is a distributed, durable, append-only commit log. Messages are written to disk and retained for a configured time whether or not anyone has read them, and each consumer group tracks its own offset, which is just a position in the log. That is why Kafka can replay, because a consumer can reset its offset and re-read retained records, and why many independent consumer groups can each get the complete stream, and why it scales to very high throughput, because appending and sequential reads are so efficient. Topics are flat, so fine-grained routing happens on the consumer side.

RabbitMQ is a traditional message broker built on the AMQP exchange-and-queue model. A producer publishes to an exchange, and the exchange routes the message into queues based on bindings and the routing key, with direct, topic, fanout, and headers exchanges giving rich broker-side routing. Consumers read from queues, and once a message is acknowledged it is removed, so by default there is no replay. RabbitMQ typically gives very low per-message latency and has first-class features Kafka lacks, like per-message time-to-live, priority queues, and simple request-reply RPC.

So the decision follows the workload. I choose Kafka for event streaming, event sourcing, big-data pipelines, log aggregation, and anywhere I need durability, replay, very high throughput, or multiple independent consumers of the same stream. I choose RabbitMQ for task and work queues where each job is handled once by one worker, for request-reply RPC, for low-latency single-message delivery, and when I need complex broker-side routing, priorities, or per-message expiry.

At National Bank of India I used both deliberately. Kafka was the event backbone: the analytics, fraud, and ledger teams each read the full transaction stream from their own offsets, and the ledger team could replay a month of events to rebuild a view. RabbitMQ handled loan-processing tasks: an exchange routed each application by a routing key into an urgent or normal queue, a worker pool consumed each task exactly once and acknowledged it so it disappeared, urgent applications used a priority queue, and a quote request used request-reply. The senior nuance I add is that each can imitate the other poorly, Kafka can emulate a work queue with a consumer group but lacks per-message priority and fine routing, and RabbitMQ can emulate pub-sub with fanout but is not built for long retention, replay, or log-level throughput, so rather than force one tool, many banks run Kafka as the streaming backbone and RabbitMQ for targeted task routing and RPC.

keyPoints: Kafka vs RabbitMQ: log-based vs message broker, persistence vs routing
Kafka vs SQS: self-managed vs managed, ordering vs simplicity
Kafka vs Pulsar: similar architecture, Pulsar has tiered storage
Choose based on: throughput, ordering, retention, operational complexity
